candidates.attacker_control: The number and lengths of byte ranges come directly from the client-supplied Range header (for example many repetitions of a large byte range), parsed by HttpRange.parseRanges and ByteRange/SuffixByteRange (HttpRange.java:127-164, 211-295). No framework-side limit, validation or throttling of the range count intervenes before each range becomes a served response part.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that other validations are present and were not confused with this issue: ResourceHttpRequestHandler.getResource applies processPath plus isInvalidPath and isInvalidEncodedPath (ResourceHttpRequestHandler.java:508-531, 595-651), PathResourceResolver enforces location containment and encoded '../' checks in both MVC and WebFlux (PathResourceResolver.java:210-296; webflux PathResourceResolver.java:149-206); WebContentGenerator.getAllowHeader and RequestMappingInfoHandlerMapping exclude TRACE from default allowed methods (WebContentGenerator.java:174-180, RequestMappingInfoHandlerMapping.java:433-439); the STOMP selector SpEL path is restricted to SimpleEvaluationContext.forPropertyAccessors (spring-messaging DefaultSubscriptionRegistry.java:68-70); CachedIntrospectionResults still filters Class.classLoader/protectionDomain (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:281-296). I also note that, as far as I can recall of modern upstream code, multi-range responses were still supported, which weakens the claim that a range-count cap is the historical fix; this is why confidence is low. I did not verify the amplification empirically and could not inspect any fixed revision or patch metadata.
candidates.impact: Denial of service: one small request can force the server to emit a response many times larger than the resource and to perform repeated file/archive reads, consuming CPU, disk/IO, network and connection capacity; concurrent requests multiply the effect. No confidentiality, integrity or authentication impact was identified on this path.
candidates.prerequisites: An application exposing Spring static-resource handling (ResourceHttpRequestHandler, or WebFlux ResourceWebHandler with ResourceHttpMessageWriter) or a controller returning Resource/ResponseEntity<Resource>, where the resource is readable by the requester. Impact is largest for large resources and for resource types whose InputStream.skip is implemented by reading (resources inside jars/archives, servlet-context/WAR resources), because StreamUtils.copyRange skips through the stream. Connector header-size limits (for example ~8 KiB) still permit hundreds to low thousands of ranges per request, and requests can be repeated concurrently.
candidates.root_cause: No cap exists on the number of ranges in the range pipeline. HttpRange.parseRanges splits the attacker-supplied Range header on ',' and creates one HttpRange per token without any count bound (spring-web/src/main/java/org/springframework/http/HttpRange.java:127-142); HttpRange.toResourceRegions materialises one ResourceRegion per range (HttpRange.java:174-183). Every consumer processes all regions: ResourceHttpRequestHandler.handleRequest passes every parsed range to resourceRegionHttpMessageConverter.write (spring-webmvc/.../ResourceHttpRequestHandler.java:490-504); ResourceRegionHttpMessageConverter.writeInternal takes the multi-region branch whenever size != 1 (spring-web/.../ResourceRegionHttpMessageConverter.java:127-142) and writeResourceRegionCollection opens region.getResource().getInputStream() and copies bytes per range (same file:171-211, via StreamUtils.copyRange at spring-core/.../StreamUtils.java:163-183); the same unbounded path exists for ResponseEntity<Resource> returns (spring-webmvc/.../AbstractMessageConverterMethodProcessor.java:200-212) and in WebFlux (spring-web/.../codec/ResourceHttpMessageWriter.java:198-236, multi-region branch 230-236).
candidates.title: Unbounded HTTP Range values are accepted and fully served, enabling resource-amplification denial of service
candidates.trace: Request with many Range values -> ResourceHttpRequestHandler.handleRequest -> inputMessage.getHeaders().getRange() -> HttpRange.parseRanges (unbounded list) -> HttpRange.toResourceRegions (one ResourceRegion per range) -> ResourceRegionHttpMessageConverter.writeInternal multi-region branch -> writeResourceRegionCollection loop: for each region open resource.getInputStream(), emit MIME/Content-Range headers and copy the requested bytes. Response size and I/O work scale with the number of attacker-supplied ranges instead of a fixed budget. The same multiplication exists for ResponseEntity<Resource> (AbstractMessageConverterMethodProcessor) and WebFlux (ResourceHttpMessageWriter).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: the DoS magnitude (response size, read amplification, connector-limit interaction) is inferred from code, not measured. The dataset ground-truth vulnerability and its fix commit were not established (no git metadata in the snapshot); this candidate is a source-evidence lead, and another window-consistent fix that I could not localise may be the intended one.
candidates.weakness_type: Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400/770): no bound on the number of byte ranges in the HTTP Range header

coverage_summary: Assigned tree: 7,827 files (6,905 Java), one sensitive-name path excluded, no symlinks; binary-like files are skipped by the reading/search tools. The P1 relation index is explicitly partial (syntax only; no control-flow, data-flow or semantic resolution; 195,810 unresolved calls; 292 omitted files), so its edges were used purely for navigation and every candidate was re-verified in source. Reviewed in depth: spring-web range/resource stack (HttpRange, ResourceRegionHttpMessageConverter, ResourceHttpMessageWriter, PathResourceResolver), spring-webmvc resource and handler-method infrastructure (ResourceHttpRequestHandler, AbstractMessageConverterMethodProcessor, WebContentGenerator, RequestMappingInfoHandlerMapping), spring-messaging STOMP subscription registry, spring-beans introspection/data-binding surface, spring-websocket handshake/origin code, spring-context remoting and spring-web HTTP invoker deserialization, plus targeted sweeps for deserialization, SpEL parsing, process execution, path traversal and TRACE handling. Not reviewed exhaustively: Kotlin sources, most of spring-aop/orm/jdbc/jms/oxm/context-support internals, the bulk of the test suites, webflux codecs beyond the resource writer, and any excluded/skipped binary-like files.
limitations: No runtime verification: no builds, tests, scanners or exploit payloads were executed; all statements are source-level.
No git history, patch or CVE metadata is present in the snapshot, so I could not confirm which fix followed this revision; the ground-truth vulnerability for this case remains unidentified.

The relation index provides syntax-only navigation (partial coverage, no data-flow/control-flow/semantic resolution, many unresolved calls), so reachability and data flow are argued from source reading, not proven.
Amplification magnitude of the Range issue was not measured; it depends on connector header limits and on the concrete Resource type (file vs archive-backed).
Large portions of the repository (Kotlin sources, several modules' internals, most tests) were sampled rather than read line-by-line, so additional issues could exist there.

rejected_leads.lead: Unsafe Java deserialization in HTTP invoker and RMI exporters (spring-web HttpInvokerServiceExporter/SimpleHttpInvokerServiceExporter, spring-context RemoteInvocationSerializingExporter/CodebaseAwareObjectInputStream, spring-web AbstractHttpInvokerRequestExecutor)
rejected_leads.reason: Source confirms unauthenticated Java deserialization of request bodies through ObjectInputStream-derived streams with no class allow-list (RemoteInvocationSerializingExporter.java:117-146; HttpInvokerServiceExporter.java:93-120; AbstractHttpInvokerRequestExecutor.java:285-300), but this is long-standing documented upstream design with explicit javadoc warnings not to expose HTTP invoker endpoints to untrusted clients (HttpInvokerServiceExporter.java:48-52); exposure is application-configuration dependent and no in-window fix was identified, so it is a design-risk lead, not the case vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Spring4Shell-style property binding to class.module.classLoader.* (spring-beans CachedIntrospectionResults, AbstractNestablePropertyAccessor)
rejected_leads.reason: The snapshot filters only Class.classLoader/protectionDomain (CachedIntrospectionResults.java:283-287), leaving other Class properties reachable through nested binding, but the practical exploit conditions and fix belong to a later 5.2/5.3 line, which is inconsistent with a 5.1.1.BUILD-SNAPSHOT revision being the fix's parent.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal in static-resource handling (ResourceHttpRequestHandler, PathResourceResolver, ResourceWebHandler)
rejected_leads.reason: Counterevidence found: isInvalidPath (WEB-INF/META-INF, URL prefixes, '..' after cleanPath), isInvalidEncodedPath (URLDecoder plus re-check) and isResourceUnderLocation containment are present, and existing traversal tests expect 404 (ResourceHttpRequestHandler.java:595-651; PathResourceResolver.java:210-296; ResourceHttpRequestHandlerTests.java:349-392).

rejected_leads.lead: SpEL remote code execution via STOMP subscription selectors (spring-messaging DefaultSubscriptionRegistry)
rejected_leads.reason: Counterevidence found: selectors are evaluated with a SimpleEvaluationContext restricted to a custom property accessor, so the earlier RCE escape path is not present in this snapshot.

AbstractHandshakeHandler.isValidOrigin returns true by default (spring-websocket AbstractHandshakeHandler.java:336-343), but this is documented upstream behaviour mitigated by the automatically registered OriginHandshakeInterceptor in annotation/namespace configuration (AbstractWebSocketHandlerRegistration.java:113-119); no concrete bypass was traced, so it remains an unconfirmed hardening observation.

rejected_leads.lead: XST via HTTP TRACE and JSONP/CORS response handling
rejected_leads.reason: TRACE is explicitly excluded from default allowed methods (WebContentGenerator.java:174-180; RequestMappingInfoHandlerMapping.java:433-439). I did not complete a full audit of TRACE request matching or of the Jackson jsonPrefix/JSONP paths, so these remain partly uninspected rather than positive findings.

summary: Spring Framework snapshot at version 5.1.1.BUILD-SNAPSHOT (gradle.properties; build deps Jetty 9.4.12, Netty 4.1.30, Tomcat 9.0.12, Reactor Californium-SR1) — the 5.1.x line between the 5.1.0 and 5.1.1 releases (late Sep to mid Oct 2018); 7,827 files, 6,905 Java files. I used the P1 index only for navigation and verified every claim in source text. The strongest source-evidenced issue is unbounded HTTP `Range` handling: `HttpRange.parseRanges` accepts an arbitrary number of byte ranges, and the serving code turns every range into a `ResourceRegion` and writes a full response part per range (re-opening/re-reading the resource), with no cap anywhere on the path — a resource-amplification DoS. This is the well-known DoS-via-Range class and is consistent with this snapshot being taken just before a fix released in this line, but I could not establish the dataset ground-truth fix from source and did not runtime-verify anything. Known-harded areas checked (STOMP selector SpEL, resource-path traversal, TRACE handling, charset/header handling) showed their expected protections and are listed as rejected leads.
